cards.s: Merge conflicts in depth
cards.html: A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines of a file (or one deletes a file the other changes). Git merges everything it can; for the rest it stops and asks you (Figure 7). Conflicts are normal. They are not errors, and you cannot break anything as long as you know how to abort.

cards.s: Hands-on: create and resolve a conflict
cards.html:
Try it: Conflict lab, about 10 minutes

Run this in an empty folder. It creates a repository where main and a feature branch disagree about one line.

terminal:

mkdir conflict-lab && cd conflict-lab && git init -b main
printf 'model: gbm\nthreshold: 0.5\nfeatures: 8\n' > config.yaml
git add . && git commit -m "chore: initial config"

git switch -c feature/stricter
printf 'model: gbm\nthreshold: 0.7\nfeatures: 8\n' > config.yaml
git commit -am "feat: stricter threshold"

git switch main            # meanwhile, a teammate changes main ...
printf 'model: gbm\nthreshold: 0.6\nfeatures: 8\n' > config.yaml
git commit -am "feat: tune threshold"

git switch feature/stricter
git merge main

expected output:

cards.s: Hands-on: create and resolve a conflict
cards.html:
Auto-merging config.yaml
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yaml
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

git status now lists config.yaml under "Unmerged paths". Open it:

config.yaml (with merge.conflictStyle zdiff3):

model: gbm
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold: 0.7
||||||| aecf8e0
threshold: 0.5
=======
threshold: 0.6
>>>>>>> main
features: 8

cards.s: Hands-on: create and resolve a conflict
cards.html:
Reading the markers: between <<<<<<< HEAD and ||||||| is your version (the branch you are on, HEAD). Between ||||||| and ======= is the base: the line as it was in the common ancestor aecf8e0. Between ======= and >>>>>>> main is the version being merged in. Without zdiff3, the middle section is missing, and you only see two different numbers without knowing who changed what.

Resolving means: edit the file into the final state you want, delete all three marker lines, then tell Git you are done:

terminal:

cards.s: Hands-on: create and resolve a conflict
cards.html:
# edit config.yaml so that it reads: threshold: 0.7
git add config.yaml          # "this file is resolved"
git commit                   # completes the merge (message prepared)
uv run pytest                # never skip this after a conflict

In VS Code, conflicted files show four small links above each conflict: Accept Current Change (yours), Accept Incoming Change (theirs), Accept Both Changes, Compare Changes. For larger conflicts click Resolve in Merge Editor: a three-pane view with incoming, current, and the result at the bottom. When the result is right, click Complete Merge, which stages the file for you.

Changed your mind? git merge --abort restores the state before the merge, as if nothing had happened.

cards.s: A harder conflict: why the base matters
cards.html:
Real conflicts rarely involve one line. Make the lab a little more realistic: on the feature branch, commit two changes (threshold 0.7, then features 10); on main, one commit changes threshold to 0.6 and features to 9. Merging gives:

config.yaml (real output):

model: gbm
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold: 0.7
features: 10
||||||| aecf8e0
threshold: 0.5
features: 8
=======
threshold: 0.6
features: 9
>>>>>>> main

cards.s: A harder conflict: why the base matters
cards.html:
Neither "accept current" nor "accept incoming" is right here. Read it as three questions:

  1. What did my side intend? Base → HEAD: threshold 0.5 → 0.7 and features 8 → 10.
  2. What did their side intend? Base → main: threshold 0.5 → 0.6 and features 8 → 9.
  3. Which intentions are compatible? Talk to the teammate, or read their commit (git log main -1 -p -- config.yaml). Perhaps they added a ninth feature column to the data, and you added a tenth on your side. Then the right answer is 11, a number neither side wrote. This is why a conflict is a question for a human, not a choice between two buttons.

cards.s: A harder conflict: why the base matters
cards.html:
Three commands that help while you are in the middle of a merge:

CommandShows
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=UOnly the files that are still conflicted.
git log --merge --oneline -- <file>The commits on both sides that touched this file: who to ask.
git diffDuring a conflict: a combined diff of the remaining conflict regions against both sides.

cards.s: Conflicts during a rebase
cards.html:
Undo the merge (git merge --abort) and run git rebase main instead. Git replays your two commits one at a time. The first one already conflicts. This is the real output:

expected output:

Rebasing (1/2)Auto-merging config.yaml
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yaml
error: could not apply aea4639... feat: stricter threshold
hint: Resolve all conflicts manually, mark them as resolved with
hint: "git add/rm <conflicted_files>", then run "git rebase --continue".
hint: You can instead skip this commit: run "git rebase --skip".
hint: To abort and get back to the state before "git rebase", run
hint: "git rebase --abort".

config.yaml during the rebase, commit 1 of 2:

cards.s: Conflicts during a rebase
cards.html:
model: gbm
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold: 0.6
features: 9
||||||| parent of aea4639 (feat: stricter threshold)
threshold: 0.5
features: 8
=======
threshold: 0.7
features: 8
>>>>>>> aea4639 (feat: stricter threshold)

cards.s: Conflicts during a rebase
cards.html:
Compare this with the merge and notice three differences:

  1. Ours and theirs are swapped. During a rebase, HEAD is main plus the commits replayed so far; the "incoming" side is your commit being replayed. In VS Code, Accept Incoming therefore keeps your change, and git checkout --theirs means your version. This trips up everyone at least once.
  2. Only one commit's change is in play. The incoming side shows features 8, because your first commit did not touch features. You resolve the intention of this commit only: threshold 0.7, keep main's features 9.
  3. Conflicts come per commit. git status tells you where you are:

expected output:

cards.s: Conflicts during a rebase
cards.html:
interactive rebase in progress; onto e8e8788
Last command done (1 command done):
   pick aea4639 # feat: stricter threshold
Next command to do (1 remaining command):
   pick 9be1d5a # feat: use 10 features

terminal:

# edit to: threshold 0.7 / features 9
git add config.yaml
git rebase --continue     # replay the next commit
# git rebase --skip       # drop this commit entirely
# git rebase --abort      # back to where you were before the rebase

cards.s: Conflicts during a rebase
cards.html:
Git now replays commit 2 and stops again, this time only on the features line (base 8, main 9, your commit 10). You resolve it, git add, --continue, and the rebase is done. Two small, focused conflicts instead of one mixed one: this is the real advantage of rebasing with small commits.

Concept: git rerere: reuse recorded resolution

If you rebase a long-lived branch several times, you meet the same conflict again and again. git config --global rerere.enabled true makes Git remember how you resolved a conflict and apply the same resolution automatically next time. You still review and git add.

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
Not every conflict has markers in a text file. git status shows a two-letter code per file (git status --short); the type decides how you resolve.

TypeStatusHow to resolve
Both modifiedUUEdit the markers away, git add.
Modify/deleteUD / DUDecide whether the file should exist. Keep it: git add <file>. Delete it: git rm <file>.
Both addedAATwo branches created the same path. Merge the contents by hand like UU.
Binary fileUUNo markers possible. Pick a side: git checkout --ours∣--theirs <file>, then git add.
Generated fileUUNever hand-edit. Resolve the source, then regenerate (lock files, below).

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What if… one branch deleted a file that the other changed?

What happens: Real output from the lab, where main removed legacy.py and the feature branch fixed a bug in it:

CONFLICT (modify/delete): legacy.py deleted in main and modified
in HEAD.  Version HEAD of legacy.py left in tree.

git status --short shows UD legacy.py. There are no markers: the file is just there, in your version.

Why: Git cannot know whether the deletion or the fix is more important.

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What you do: Find out why it was deleted (git log main -1 -- legacy.py). Usually the code moved somewhere: then git rm legacy.py and apply your bug fix in the new location, in the same merge commit. Only if the deletion was a mistake: git add legacy.py.

What if… uv.lock (or poetry.lock, package-lock.json) conflicts?

What happens: You added rich, a teammate added tabulate. Both pyproject.toml and uv.lock conflict. Lock files are huge generated files; their conflict regions are meaningless to a human, and uv cannot even read a lock file with markers in it.

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What you do: Resolve the input by hand, then regenerate the output. This sequence was run in the lab:

# 1. pyproject.toml: keep BOTH dependencies, delete the markers
#    dependencies = ["rich>=15.0.0", "tabulate>=0.10.0"]
git checkout --theirs uv.lock   # any consistent version as a start
uv lock                         # re-resolve from pyproject.toml
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock
uv sync --locked                # proves lock and pyproject agree
git commit

If you forget uv lock, CI fails at uv sync --locked with the error The lockfile at uv.lock needs to be updated, but --locked was provided., which is exactly what that flag is for.

What if… a Jupyter notebook conflicts?

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What happens: A .ipynb file is JSON with code, outputs, execution counts and base64 images. Two people running the same notebook create conflicts even without changing code, and the markers break the JSON so the notebook will not open.

What you do: Prevention beats cure: strip outputs before commit (nbstripout --install adds a Git filter; there is also a pre-commit hook), and move reusable code from notebooks into .py modules that are tested. When it happens anyway, nbdime gives a notebook-aware merge tool (nbdime config-git --enable, then git mergetool --tool nbdime), or take one side with git checkout --ours and re-apply the other change by hand.

What if… a trained model file or other binary conflicts?

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What happens: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in models/model.joblib; Git cannot merge bytes.

Why: Two branches each committed a retrained model.

What you do: Pick a side (git checkout --theirs models/model.joblib) and, better, retrain from the merged code and data. The real fix is structural: model files do not belong in Git. In this book, CI trains the model and the image or the MLflow registry stores it; Git stores the code and configuration that produce it.

What if… the merge has no conflicts, but the result is broken?

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What happens: This was reproduced in a lab. Branch rename renames scale() to normalise() and updates every caller. Branch newcall adds report.py, which calls scale(). Both merge into main with exit code 0. Then:

report.py:1: in <module>
    from features import scale
E   ImportError: cannot import name 'scale' from 'features'
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Interrupted: 1 error during collection !!!!!!!!!!

Why: Git merges text, not meaning. The two changes touched different files, so there was nothing to conflict about in Git's eyes. This is a semantic conflict.

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html:
What you do: This is the strongest argument for CI on the merged result: run tests after every merge locally, require "branches up to date" or a merge queue on GitHub (Level 2), and run CI on every push to main. Git can never catch this; only tests can.

What if… I resolved a conflict wrong and already committed the merge?

cards.s: A field guide to conflict types
cards.html: What you do: Not pushed yet: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (or HEAD~1) returns to before the merge; merge again. Already pushed to a shared branch: do not rewrite. Make a normal follow-up commit that fixes the resolution ("fix forward"), or git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> if the whole merge must go (read the revert trap in Section 2.7 first). To see what you actually decided during the resolution, git show <merge-sha> displays only the lines where the merge result differs from both parents.

cards.s: Avoiding conflicts
cards.html:
• Keep branches short-lived (one to three days) and PRs small.
  • Rebase on main daily, so conflicts are small when they appear.
  • Let a formatter (ruff) own the code style; then nobody creates diffs by re-indenting.
  • Avoid "hot" files everybody edits, such as one giant config.py; split them.
  • Talk: if you and a colleague both need to refactor the same module, agree on an order.
